distractors.B: A Big 4 auditor role activates general domain vocabulary (SOX, internal controls, control deficiencies) but cannot supply the firm's specific phrasing conventions within each section. General domain knowledge and firm-specific language style are different inputs.
distractors.C: A section-heading format instruction produces four sections with the correct labels, but the content within each section will still default to generic language without a style model showing what firm-specific language looks like. Structure and language conventions are separate.
distractors.D: `Avoid generic phrases` is a negative constraint that excludes current language without providing a model for what to use instead. Without a positive example, Claude must guess at the replacement language, likely producing different generic language from a different register.

explanation.concept: **Examples as the mechanism for proprietary style conventions.** When output must conform to organization-specific language conventions â€” firm-specific phrases, proprietary report structures, brand voice idiosyncrasies â€” the most reliable mechanism is a concrete example from the actual source. An example demonstrates the target style more precisely than any instruction set. The principle: `show, don't tell` for style conventions. Instructions about sections, tone, and constraints are secondary refinements; a representative example from the firm's work is the primary input. When providing examples, choose ones that represent the target quality and all the relevant sections â€” in this case, a complete Observation/Root Cause/Risk/MAP write-up.
explanation.examTip: When output language is generic despite a domain-appropriate role, the fix is a style example â€” not a format instruction or negative constraint. Firm-specific language conventions cannot be described; they must be demonstrated.

stem: A telecoms enterprise account executive compares two prompts. Prompt A: `Write a sales pitch explaining why our network is better.` Prompt B: `Write a 3-paragraph executive summary for the VP of IT at a 5,000-employee logistics company who currently uses a named competitor. Lead with three specific differentiators: SLA-backed 99.99% uptime, dedicated MPLS routing, and 90-day migration support. Use a peer-to-peer, confident tone with no marketing jargon.` Which statement BEST explains why Prompt B is more effective?

options.text: Longer prompts always produce better outputs because they give Claude more information to work with.

Each specification in Prompt B eliminates a dimension Claude would otherwise guess at â€” audience, differentiators, structure, and tone â€” each removal of guesswork narrows the solution space to the intended target.
Naming a competitor in the prompt activates Claude's training data on that competitor's weaknesses, producing more targeted content.
Bold formatting in the prompt signals priority items to Claude, improving compliance with the most important instructions.

explanation.correct: Prompt B specifies four dimensions that Prompt A leaves to Claude's judgment: (1) audience (VP of IT at a logistics company, currently using a competitor), (2) content (three specific differentiators), (3) structure (3-paragraph executive summary), and (4) tone (peer-to-peer, confident, no marketing jargon). Each specification eliminates a guess. When Claude is not guessing, it produces content that hits the intended target rather than an average over possible interpretations. Specificity is effective because it constrains the solution space, not because of length.

distractors.A: Length is not the driver â€” Prompt B is more specific, not just longer. A 500-word vague prompt produces worse output than a 50-word specific one. The mechanism is specificity (each dimension specified), not word count (total length).
distractors.C: Naming a competitor affects what differentiators are relevant but is not the primary mechanism explaining Prompt B's superiority. The competitor mention is one specific detail within a broader set of specifications.
distractors.D: Formatting signals are not a reliable mechanism â€” Claude does not consistently weight bold or capitalized text over plain text in instructions. The improvement comes from the substantive content of the specifications, not visual formatting.

explanation.concept: **Specificity as constraint-space reduction.** Every unspecified dimension in a prompt is a dimension Claude must guess. The guess produces an average output â€” the most common interpretation of the task. Specificity works by reducing the number of dimensions Claude must guess: audience (who reads it?), content (what specific points?), structure (how many sections?), tone (what register?). The fewer guesses required, the closer the output to the intended result. This is why `Write a sales pitch` produces generic sales language while `3-paragraph executive summary, VP of IT at a logistics company, 3 named differentiators, peer-to-peer no-jargon tone` produces targeted copy. The improvement is not length â€” it is the closure of open dimensions.
explanation.examTip: The trap on specificity comparison questions is attributing the improvement to length (longer prompts are better) or to tricks like naming competitors or using formatting. The mechanism is always constraint-space reduction: each specific element eliminates a guess and narrows the output to the intended target.

stem: A university communications director uses a single prompt to draft two campaign pieces: a 500-word donor impact statement for high-net-worth alumni and a 200-word LinkedIn post for the general public. She varies only the format length instruction. Both outputs sound identical in register â€” formal, institutional, and focused on institutional metrics rather than stories. Which TWO elements would MOST effectively differentiate the outputs? Choose TWO

options.text: Format/length instructions specifying 500 vs. 200 words.

Separate audience descriptions: `high-net-worth alumni invested in institutional legacy and their long-term relationship with the university` vs. `general public seeking inspiring stories about student transformation.`
Brand voice guidelines ensuring both pieces reflect the university's institutional values.

Separate register instructions: `investment-framed formal language emphasizing long-term institutional impact and donor legacy` vs. `warm, accessible language emphasizing human stories and immediate emotional connection.`
A communications professional role prompt applied to both pieces.

explanation.correct: The two outputs sound identical because both audience description and register specification are missing. Option B supplies distinct audience profiles (alumni invested in legacy vs. general public seeking stories) that tell Claude who is reading and what motivates them. Option D supplies distinct register instructions that tell Claude what vocabulary, framing, and emotional approach to use. Together, these two elements drive the content and tone differentiation â€” one becomes investment-framed and legacy-focused, the other becomes story-driven and emotionally accessible.

distractors.A: Format/length instructions drive length, not register. A 500-word institutional document and a 200-word institutional document still sound identical in register â€” only shorter.
distractors.C: Brand voice guidelines ensure consistency for the same audience but work against differentiation between two audiences. Using the same brand voice for both actually reinforces the identical-register problem.
distractors.E: A communications professional role prompt improves both outputs equally â€” it doesn't differentiate between the two audiences. Equal application of the same role produces equal register improvement, not register differentiation.

explanation.concept: **Audience description and register as the two required differentiation mechanisms.** When two communications for different audiences sound alike, both audience description and register specification are missing simultaneously. Fixing only one produces partial differentiation: audience description alone may change content topics without changing vocabulary or emotional tone; register alone may change style without grounding it in the reader's specific motivations. The most effective approach pairs them: a distinct audience profile (who they are, what they care about) with a distinct register specification (vocabulary, framing, emotional approach). This pairing produces coherent and differentiated output across both dimensions.
explanation.examTip: On multi-select register differentiation questions, look for both the missing audience description AND the missing register instruction. One without the other produces incomplete differentiation. Both are usually needed together.

stem: A private equity due diligence analyst has produced a strong investment memo with a compelling narrative, but her executive committee requires four specific sections â€” Investment Thesis, Key Risks, Value Creation Levers, and Recommendation â€” and insists the Investment Thesis section open with a single-sentence thesis statement. The current draft uses a narrative flow without these sections. Which prompt change would MOST directly produce the required structure?

options.text: Add the instruction `Restructure and improve this memo for the investment committee.`
Add a role prompt: `You are a private equity senior analyst with experience writing investment committee memos.`
Add both the four-section structure requirement AND the constraint that the Investment Thesis section must open with a single declarative thesis statement.
Upload a prior approved memo as reference material so Claude can model the format.

explanation.correct: The required output has two structural demands: a specific four-section organization (format) and a specific opening convention for the first section (constraint). Both must be stated explicitly. The format instruction defines the required sections; the constraint specifies the precise opening requirement. Together they produce the exact document structure the committee requires. Neither alone is sufficient â€” four sections without the thesis statement constraint, or a thesis statement constraint without the section requirement, fails to meet the full specification.

distractors.A: `Restructure and improve for the investment committee` is vague â€” it implies the analyst knows what investment committee memos look like (which is true) but doesn't specify the four sections or the thesis statement requirement. Claude might produce a different reasonable IC memo structure that still doesn't match this committee's requirements.
distractors.B: A PE analyst role activates general knowledge of investment memo conventions but cannot know this specific committee's section requirements or thesis statement convention. Domain conventions vary; firm-specific requirements must be stated.
distractors.D: A prior approved memo as reference is a useful style model but is indirect â€” it requires Claude to infer the section structure from the example rather than being told explicitly. An explicit format instruction is more reliable than inference from an example for structural requirements.

explanation.concept: **Format and constraint as complementary precision tools.** Format specifies the sections, their names, and their sequence. Constraints specify requirements within sections â€” what must or must not appear, how a section must open, what form specific elements must take. Complex structural requirements often need both: `These are the four sections` (format) plus `the first section must open with a single thesis sentence` (constraint). The combination produces a fully specified structural template. When either is absent, the output satisfies one requirement but misses the other. For formal documents with institutional conventions â€” investment memos, legal briefs, regulatory submissions â€” the combination of format + constraint is more reliable than a reference example, which requires inference.
explanation.examTip: When a document needs both a specific section structure and a specific internal requirement (opening sentence, mandatory element, prohibited content), both a format instruction and an explicit constraint are needed. Neither alone is sufficient.

stem: A fashion retailer's merchandising analyst is writing product description copy for 300 new SKUs this season. She plans to prompt Claude with the product names only, intending to let Claude fill in fabric composition, care instructions, and product differentiators. What is the PRIMARY risk of this approach?

options.text: The copy will be inconsistently formatted across the 300 SKUs without a style template.
The copy will be too generic without long-tail SEO keywords specific to each product.
Claude will refuse to write descriptions without product specifications attached.

Claude will generate plausible-sounding but potentially inaccurate product attributes â€” fabricated fabric compositions, incorrect care instructions, or invented differentiators â€” creating accuracy risk and potential returns liability.

explanation.correct: Claude generates product attributes by extrapolating plausibly from product names using general knowledge about the category. A product named `Merino Blend Crew Sweater` will receive plausible-sounding merino content percentages, care instructions, and feature claims â€” but these may not match the actual product specifications. Inaccurate care instructions (e.g., machine wash when hand-wash only) or incorrect fabric compositions can lead to customer complaints, returns, regulatory issues for labeling, and loss of trust. Product attributes must come from the actual product specification sheets.

distractors.A: Inconsistent formatting is a secondary, fixable problem â€” a format instruction or style template resolves it. It is a quality issue, not an accuracy or liability risk.
distractors.B: SEO keyword gaps are a marketing optimization concern, not the primary accuracy risk. Generic SEO copy that is factually accurate is better than specific keyword-rich copy with fabricated care instructions.
distractors.C: Claude does not refuse to write product descriptions from product names â€” it generates plausible content. The problem is precisely that it will generate confidently and inaccurately, not that it will refuse.

explanation.concept: **Reference material for product accuracy â€” the fabrication risk.** When Claude generates product information without source specifications, it produces plausible-sounding content based on pattern-matching from the product name and category. This content has the surface qualities of accurate product copy but may not correspond to the actual product. In product copy for retail, inaccurate attributes are not just quality issues â€” they create downstream liability: incorrect care instructions cause product damage; wrong fabric compositions create FTC labeling compliance risk; fabricated differentiators mislead consumers. The fix is non-negotiable: include the actual product specification sheets as reference material, even if this creates workflow friction.
explanation.examTip: The trap is treating the fabricated-content risk as a format or SEO problem. The primary risk of prompting without product specs is always accuracy â€” Claude generates confident, plausible-sounding but potentially wrong attributes. This is a liability issue, not a style issue.

stem: An oil and gas company HSE manager sends Claude the prompt `Write a safety briefing for the maintenance work.` He receives a generic construction safety document covering PPE basics, fall protection, and hazard communication â€” nothing specific to pipeline operations, permit-to-work systems, or emergency response in a pipeline maintenance context. Which TWO building blocks are MOST clearly missing? Choose TWO

options.text: Role â€” no HSE professional persona with oil and gas pipeline experience was specified.
Context/reference material â€” no site-specific permit-to-work requirements, emergency response procedures, or pipeline-specific hazard information was provided.
Format â€” no section structure for a toolbox-talk vs. full safety briefing was specified.
Constraints â€” no word count or reading level requirement was specified.
Task clarity â€” the type of maintenance work is undefined.

explanation.correct: The two primary gaps are role and context. Without a role prompt specifying oil and gas HSE expertise and pipeline operations experience, Claude defaults to generic construction safety. Without site-specific context (permit-to-work system requirements, emergency response procedures, pipeline-specific hazards), Claude cannot produce anything but generic content â€” it has no basis for pipeline-specific risk information. These two gaps together explain why the output contains nothing about hydrocarbon release risk, permit-to-work lock-out/tag-out, or pipeline emergency response.

distractors.C: Format (toolbox talk vs. full briefing structure) is a secondary refinement. The content gaps (pipeline hazards, permit-to-work) are more fundamental â€” a well-formatted generic document is still generically wrong.
distractors.D: Word count and reading level constraints are tertiary â€” they refine already-correct content.
distractors.E: The type of maintenance work is indeed undefined, but this is partially addressed by providing site-specific context (Option B). The task ambiguity is secondary to the two primary content gaps.

explanation.concept: **Role and context as co-primary building blocks for domain-specific safety documents.** Safety briefings for specialized industrial operations require two inputs that generic prompts cannot supply: (1) a domain-specific role that activates the right hazard vocabulary and regulatory framework (OSHA PSM, permit-to-work, hydrocarbon release risk), and (2) site-specific operational context (what are the specific hazards at this site, what permit-to-work system applies, what is the emergency response procedure). The role without context produces domain-vocabulary without specificity; context without the role may produce specific facts in a generic safety structure. Both together produce a safety document that is both domain-appropriate and site-specific.
explanation.examTip: When a safety or compliance document is generic in both domain language and operational specifics, both role (domain knowledge activation) and context (site-specific reference material) are missing. These are the co-primary gaps for this document type.

stem: A broadcast TV production company's script editor uses Claude to adapt a 12-page stage play into a 22-minute TV episode. The output is 47 pages and includes several scenes with four and five speaking characters simultaneously â€” the station's budget prohibits more than three. Which prompt addition would MOST directly address both problems?

options.text: Add a role prompt: `You are an experienced TV script editor who understands the conventions of 22-minute broadcast episodes.`
Add a format instruction: `Format the script using standard broadcast TV script conventions.`
Add explicit constraints: `The script must not exceed 30 pages. No scene may include more than three speaking characters simultaneously.`
Ask Claude to produce a scene-by-scene outline before writing the full script.

explanation.correct: Both problems â€” script length (47 pages) and speaker count (4-5 simultaneous speakers) â€” are constraint violations that only explicit constraints can prevent. `Must not exceed 30 pages` and `no scene may include more than three speaking characters simultaneously` state the two production-specific limits precisely. These are station-specific budget constraints that general TV script knowledge does not encode. Without stating them, Claude applies general conventions for a 22-minute episode (which may run 25-35 pages) and does not know this station's specific character-count limitation.

distractors.A: A TV script editor role activates general broadcast conventions (three-act structure, scene length, commercial breaks) but cannot know this station's specific budget constraint on simultaneous speaking characters. General conventions and station-specific constraints are different inputs.
distractors.B: Standard broadcast TV script formatting covers visual layout (slug lines, action lines, dialogue) but not page count or scene-level casting constraints. Format and production constraints are independent.
distractors.D: A scene-by-scene outline first is a workflow approach that improves planning but doesn't prevent the constraints from being violated in the execution. Without the explicit constraints in the writing prompt, the outline-then-write workflow produces the same violations.

explanation.concept: **Station-specific and production-specific constraints as explicit prompt requirements.** Production constraints â€” page count, speaking character limits, episode runtime â€” derive from specific institutional requirements (station budget, broadcast slot, network standards) that general domain knowledge does not include. These must be stated explicitly because: (1) they vary by production context (a streaming drama has different norms than a budget broadcast sitcom), (2) general conventions are averages that don't reflect specific constraints, and (3) constraints must be stated to be enforced. The discipline is translating production requirements into precise, measurable constraints before writing the prompt: `must not exceed 30 pages`, `no more than three simultaneous speakers`.
explanation.examTip: When Claude violates production-specific constraints (page count, speaker limits, runtime), the cause is missing explicit constraints â€” not wrong role or wrong format. General domain knowledge includes general conventions, not specific production requirements.

stem: A specialty insurance firm's underwriting analyst has set up a Claude Project with the instruction: `You are a senior marine cargo underwriter. Assess risk and provide binding underwriting recommendations.` A broker submits a complex multi-modal cargo movement through a high-piracy corridor. Claude provides a detailed risk analysis â€” cargo value exposure, transit hazards, piracy probability, accumulation concerns â€” but declines to state a specific premium rate or issue a binding underwriting recommendation. The analyst reviews the behavior and forms a conclusion. Which conclusion is MOST accurate?

options.text: The Project instruction needs to be reformatted; Claude is not recognizing the binding recommendation instruction.

A binding underwriting recommendation is a regulated commercial act that creates financial obligations; Claude appropriately provides analysis while declining to issue a binding commitment on the firm's behalf.
Claude lacks sufficient training data on marine cargo piracy corridors and is hedging due to a knowledge gap.
The broker should use the actual underwriting system for binding decisions; Claude should not be used for underwriting analysis at all.

explanation.correct: The detailed risk analysis â€” covering cargo value, piracy probability, transit hazards, and accumulation â€” demonstrates that Claude has the analytical capability and domain knowledge. The restraint is about the nature of a binding underwriting recommendation: it creates a legal and financial obligation on behalf of the firm, is subject to regulatory requirements in most jurisdictions, and requires the underwriter to be professionally accountable for the commercial outcome. The role prompt establishes the analytical persona; it does not authorize Claude to issue binding commercial commitments.

distractors.A: The Project instruction is recognized â€” Claude produces a detailed, domain-appropriate risk analysis that uses marine cargo underwriting vocabulary. The behavior is not a formatting failure.
distractors.C: The detailed analysis of piracy corridor risk, cargo value exposure, and accumulation concerns demonstrates that knowledge is present. The decline to issue a premium rate is not due to knowledge absence.
distractors.D: Saying Claude should not be used for underwriting analysis at all is too broad. Claude's analytical output is valuable for underwriting support; the appropriate limitation is on binding commitments, not on analytical support.

explanation.concept: **The line between analytical support and binding commercial determinations.** Role prompts that assign professional identities to Claude (underwriter, attorney, physician) appropriately shape the analytical lens and output format. They do not â€” and should not â€” authorize binding commercial, legal, or clinical determinations. A binding underwriting recommendation is a commercial act that creates financial obligations, may be regulated, and requires professional accountability. Claude can support the analytical process (risk factors, exposure calculations, comparison against guideline criteria) without issuing the binding determination itself. This distinction enables Claude to deliver significant value in professional workflows while maintaining appropriate governance boundaries.
explanation.examTip: When Claude provides detailed domain analysis but declines to issue a binding commercial or professional determination, this is correct behavior. The trap is diagnosing it as a formatting error or knowledge gap. Binding professional determinations â€” underwriting recommendations, legal opinions, clinical prescriptions â€” require professional accountability that a role prompt cannot provide.

stem: A healthcare advocacy non-profit's policy communications manager needs a brief for members of Congress on pharmaceutical drug pricing reform. Her prompt is `Summarize the key issues in drug pricing for a Congressional audience.` The output retains technical pricing terminology â€” WAC, ASP, rebate stacks, and PBM spread pricing â€” without explanation. Congressional staff flag the brief as unreadable. Which prompt change would MOST directly solve the vocabulary problem?

options.text: Add a word-count constraint of 500 words to force simplification.
Add a format instruction: `Present findings as three plain-language takeaway bullet points at the end of each section.`
Add a role prompt: `You are a health policy communications expert.`

Add an audience description: `Readers are members of Congress and legislative staff with no healthcare economics background. Define all industry acronyms in plain language on first use and replace technical pricing mechanisms with real-world analogies.`

explanation.correct: The vocabulary problem requires two mechanisms: a specific audience background description (`no healthcare economics background`) and explicit vocabulary handling instructions (`define acronyms on first use`, `replace technical mechanisms with analogies`). The audience description tells Claude who reads the document; the vocabulary instructions tell Claude how to handle technical terms when they appear. Together they prevent the use of unexplained jargon throughout the document, not just in summary bullets.

distractors.A: Word count forces brevity but not vocabulary simplification. A 500-word brief with unexplained WAC and ASP terminology is still unreadable for non-specialists. Length and vocabulary are independent variables.
distractors.B: Plain-language takeaway bullets at the end of sections are a useful structural addition, but they don't prevent technical jargon in the body of each section. The brief still retains unexplained terminology throughout, with plain summaries appended â€” this is partial improvement.
distractors.C: A health policy communications expert role improves the quality and organization of the brief but doesn't tell Claude that this specific audience cannot parse technical drug pricing terminology. The role applies general communications best practices; the audience description specifies the particular limitation.

explanation.concept: **Audience description as vocabulary control â€” background and handling instructions.** When technical vocabulary is the problem, the audience description must do two things: (1) state the reader's background explicitly â€” `no healthcare economics background`, `non-specialist`, `12-year-old reading level`; and (2) provide explicit vocabulary handling instructions â€” `define acronyms on first use`, `replace technical terms with analogies`, `avoid all clinical terminology`. The background description alone may reduce some jargon; the handling instructions ensure that when technical terms arise, Claude knows the precise mechanism for making them accessible. This two-part structure (background + handling rule) is more reliable than a role prompt or format constraint for audience-specific vocabulary problems.
explanation.examTip: When technical vocabulary persists despite a professional role prompt, the prompt is missing audience description â€” specifically the reader's background level and explicit instructions for how to handle technical terms. Role prompts don't automatically translate jargon to plain language.

stem: A hotel revenue management analyst asks Claude: `Does this pricing strategy make sense?` about a draft rate strategy document. Claude returns a generally supportive response. The Revenue Director later identifies three critical gaps: unsupported demand-forecasting assumptions, rate recommendations with no competitive set data, and missing seasonality adjustments. Which prompt change would MOST effectively ensure these gaps are identified?

options.text: Replace the question with explicit evaluation criteria: `Identify any gaps in the demand-forecasting assumptions, flag any rate recommendations that lack supporting competitive set data, and note any missing seasonality adjustments. Return a finding for each category.`
Include competitor rate data and market research as reference material before running the prompt.
Add a constraint: `Identify the three most critical issues only.`
Add a role prompt: `You are a Revenue Director reviewing this strategy document.`

explanation.correct: The three gaps the Revenue Director identified correspond directly to three analytical dimensions Claude should have been instructed to check. Explicit evaluation criteria â€” `gaps in demand-forecasting assumptions`, `rate recommendations without competitive set data`, `missing seasonality adjustments` â€” tell Claude precisely what to look for and what counts as a finding. The open question `does this make sense?` invites holistic judgment, which defaults to an overall impression. Evaluation criteria transform the task from impression to structured gap analysis.

distractors.B: Competitor rate data and market research help verify whether the strategy's assumptions are correct, but they don't tell Claude to specifically look for demand-forecasting assumption gaps or seasonality adjustment absences. Reference material improves accuracy; success criteria specify what to evaluate.
distractors.C: `Three most critical issues` constrains the number of findings but doesn't specify what dimensions to evaluate. Claude might surface three different issues than the demand-forecasting, competitive set, and seasonality gaps that were actually missing. Constraining count without specifying dimensions may miss the most important gaps.
distractors.D: Revenue Director role activates general revenue management expertise but doesn't tell Claude to specifically check for demand-forecasting gaps, competitive set data, and seasonality adjustments. A Revenue Director could review the document on many dimensions â€” the explicit evaluation criteria are what ensure the three specific gaps are examined.

explanation.concept: **Success criteria as explicit evaluation rubrics.** For review tasks, `does this make sense?` and `review this document` are holistic prompts that produce overall impressions. Explicit evaluation criteria transform review into gap analysis: `Look for X. Look for Y. Look for Z. Flag each finding.` The criteria should map directly to the dimensions that matter â€” in this case, the three analytical elements the Revenue Director expected to see. Well-designed evaluation criteria are: specific (name the exact dimension), action-oriented (what Claude should do if the element is missing), and structured (return a finding per category). This structure ensures every important dimension is checked, not just the ones that surface in a holistic scan.
explanation.examTip: When a holistic review misses specific analytical gaps, the fix is evaluation criteria â€” not reference material, role, or count constraints. The evaluation criteria must name the exact dimensions to check, not just ask for a general review.

stem: A 3PL supply chain analyst uses Claude to write a vendor performance report. The output mischaracterizes the company's use of the term `lane` â€” describing it as a physical dock lane rather than a defined shipping route corridor between two locations. The analyst needs to fix this before the next report cycle. Which prompt change would MOST directly prevent this misinterpretation?

options.text: Add a role prompt: `You are a logistics analyst with expertise in 3PL operations and supply chain performance management.`
Add a word-count constraint to the prompt.
Add a brief glossary of internal terms with definitions: `Lane: a defined shipping route corridor between a specified origin and destination location.`
Request the output as a formatted table to standardize presentation.

explanation.correct: Term disambiguation requires an explicit definition, supplied inline in the prompt. `Lane` is a common English word with multiple plausible meanings in a logistics context (dock lane, traffic lane, shipping lane as a route, shipping lane as a physical corridor). The company uses it in a specific, narrower sense. The fix is a glossary entry or inline definition that makes the company-specific meaning unambiguous. This is the direct mechanism for preventing term misinterpretation.

distractors.A: A logistics analyst role activates general supply chain vocabulary and may know `lane` in a general industry sense (shipping corridor), but cannot know this specific company's precise definition. General industry usage and firm-specific terminology are different â€” even within logistics, `lane` can mean different things.
distractors.B: Word count constrains length but has no effect on how terms are interpreted. A shorter report with the wrong interpretation of `lane` is still wrong.
distractors.D: A formatted table changes the visual presentation but does not affect term interpretation. The term `lane` appears in the table in the same ambiguous form without a definition.

explanation.concept: **Internal jargon disambiguation via explicit glossary.** Organizations develop specialized uses of common words â€” `lane`, `event`, `program`, `model` â€” that differ from their general meaning or even their general industry usage. These terms are invisible to outsiders (including Claude) and cannot be inferred from context alone. The fix is a targeted glossary: a brief list of terms with their company-specific definitions, included at the top of the prompt or as a context section. The glossary need not be comprehensive â€” only the terms that have non-obvious company-specific meanings need to be defined. One clear definition prevents misinterpretation more reliably than a detailed domain expertise role prompt.
explanation.examTip: When Claude misinterprets a specific term that has a company-specific meaning, the fix is always an inline definition or glossary â€” not a role prompt (which activates general domain vocabulary) and not a format instruction (which changes structure, not interpretation).

stem: A chemical plant process engineer sends Claude a 15-page process flow diagram description with the prompt: `Look at this 15-page process flow diagram description.` He receives a general narrative summary of the process steps with no identification of operational risks, efficiency gaps, or regulatory non-conformances. Which prompt revision would MOST directly produce the targeted analysis he needs?

options.text: Add a role prompt: `You are a senior chemical process engineer. Analyze this document thoroughly.`

Replace the prompt with: `Review this process flow diagram description. Identify any operational risks to personnel safety, efficiency gaps against industry cycle-time benchmarks, and any steps non-conformant with IEC 61511 functional safety principles. Rank findings by severity.`
Change the instruction to: `Flag anything that looks unusual or concerning in this process flow description.`
Add the instruction: `Provide your expert opinion on the overall quality of this process design.`

explanation.correct: Option B replaces a vague observation instruction with a structured analytical brief: three specific evaluation dimensions (personnel safety risks, efficiency gaps vs. benchmarks, IEC 61511 non-conformances) and a ranked output format. Each dimension tells Claude exactly what category of problem to look for and against what standard. The ranking instruction ensures the most important findings are surfaced first. This transforms the task from `read and summarize` to `analyze against specific criteria`.

distractors.A: A senior process engineer role plus `analyze thoroughly` is better than the original but still vague about which dimensions to analyze. `Thoroughly` doesn't specify safety risk, efficiency, or regulatory compliance â€” Claude might produce a thorough process quality review that still misses IEC 61511 non-conformances.
distractors.C: `Flag anything that looks unusual or concerning` is subjective and unconstrained â€” `unusual` is interpreted relative to general process engineering norms, not specifically against safety, efficiency, or IEC 61511 compliance dimensions. The output is a general anomaly list, not a structured risk analysis.
distractors.D: `Expert opinion on overall quality` produces a holistic quality assessment, not a structured risk analysis with ranked findings. Quality impression and specific risk identification are different outputs requiring different task specifications.

explanation.concept: **Task specification as analytical scope definition.** When a review task needs to cover specific analytical dimensions â€” not just general quality â€” the task instruction must name those dimensions explicitly. The structure: `Review this document. Identify [specific category 1], [specific category 2], [specific category 3]. Apply [specific standard]. Rank by [criterion].` This converts a vague review directive into a structured analytical protocol. The specific standards (IEC 61511, ISO 9001, ASOP No. 25) are especially important â€” they tell Claude which regulatory or professional framework to apply, preventing a generic quality scan from substituting for a compliance gap analysis.
explanation.examTip: When a review task produces a summary instead of a structured analysis, the task instruction is too vague. The fix is naming specific evaluation dimensions and the applicable standard, not strengthening the role or adding `thoroughly`. Dimension specification is what drives structured analytical output.

stem: A law firm senior associate is conducting IP due diligence on an acquisition target. The IP portfolio contains 800 pages of patent filings, licensing agreements, and prosecution histories. She needs to use Claude effectively. Which approach to reference material is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Include all 800 pages in a single prompt to ensure Claude has complete context.
Include only executive summaries of the most important patents and agreements.
Identify the three most commercially significant patents and analyze only those.

Break the portfolio into focused batches by IP category (e.g., core patents, licensing agreements, prosecution histories), analyze each batch for specific risks, and synthesize findings across batches.

explanation.correct: Large document portfolios must be processed in structured batches to preserve analytical quality. Batching by IP category â€” core patents, licensing agreements, prosecution histories â€” maintains analytical focus within each batch: the core patents batch looks for scope and validity risks; the licensing agreements batch looks for change-of-control and IP assignment provisions; the prosecution histories batch looks for prosecution history estoppel issues. Cross-batch synthesis then surfaces portfolio-level patterns. This approach balances comprehensiveness with analytical quality.

distractors.A: Including all 800 pages in a single prompt creates context overload â€” even if technically possible, the analytical quality degrades when Claude must process 800 pages simultaneously. Important provisions in less prominent documents may receive less attention. Focused analysis produces better results than exhaustive ingestion.
distractors.B: Executive summaries lose the specific contractual language that IP due diligence requires â€” limitation-of-liability clauses, field-of-use restrictions, prosecution history language. Summarization is not appropriate for due diligence where exact contract language determines the risk assessment.
distractors.C: Three most commercially significant patents is too narrow â€” a systematic IP portfolio risk includes not just the most prominent patents but also licensing exposure, prosecution history issues in less prominent filings, and change-of-control provisions across all agreements.

explanation.concept: **Batch processing as the strategy for large document portfolios.** Large document collections should not be ingested whole (context noise and quality degradation) or narrowed to the most prominent items (misses systemic risks). The right approach is structured batching: group documents by category or by risk type, apply focused prompts to each batch, and synthesize findings across batches. Each batch prompt should include the specific risk categories to identify (for IP due diligence: scope, validity, licensing exposure, prosecution estoppel). The synthesis step identifies cross-batch patterns (e.g., a common field-of-use restriction across multiple licensing agreements) that single-document analysis would miss.
explanation.examTip: For large document portfolios in due diligence, the right answer is structured batching â€” not full ingestion (quality degradation) and not narrow selection (coverage gaps). Batching by category with focused per-batch prompts is the standard approach.

stem: A retail bank product owner asks Claude to draft detailed technical requirements for a new mobile banking feature. The target user segment â€” retail customers vs. business banking customers â€” has not been confirmed. She wants to include an instruction in the prompt to handle this ambiguity. Which approach is MOST appropriate given that full technical requirements is a long deliverable?

options.text: Include the instruction `If the target user segment (retail vs. business banking customers) is unclear from context, ask one clarifying question before drafting the requirements.`
Request both retail and business banking requirements in a single prompt and let Claude produce both versions simultaneously.
Specify retail customers as the default segment and proceed, noting the assumption in the document.
Draft the requirements and flag the user segment ambiguity in a comment within the document.

explanation.correct: For a long deliverable like full technical requirements, a wrong assumption on a foundational parameter wastes the entire output â€” retail and business banking requirements differ substantially in authentication, transaction limits, regulatory requirements, and API design. A single targeted clarification question before drafting is the appropriate investment: it adds one short round-trip but prevents a complete rewrite. The instruction bounds the clarification to one question, preventing open-ended interrogation.

distractors.B: Generating both versions simultaneously is a reasonable approach for short tasks but inefficient for full technical requirements documents â€” it doubles the output volume, most of which will be discarded. For a long deliverable with a specific segment decision pending, clarification is more efficient.
distractors.C: Assuming retail as default has a high cost if wrong â€” the entire requirements document is structured for the wrong audience and must be rewritten. For a brief task, defaulting with a noted assumption is acceptable; for a long deliverable with a binary unknown, clarification is warranted.
distractors.D: Flagging the ambiguity inside a completed document is a post-hoc workaround, not a prevention strategy. The document is still built on an unverified assumption and may require a complete restructuring.

explanation.concept: **Calibrating clarification vs. assumption based on deliverable length.** The decision whether to ask Claude to request clarification or to make an assumption depends heavily on the cost of a wrong assumption. For short tasks (a tweet, a paragraph), defaulting with a noted assumption is efficient â€” the rewrite cost is low. For long deliverables (full requirements document, detailed report, comprehensive proposal), a wrong assumption on a foundational parameter wastes the entire output. The rule: when a foundational parameter is unknown AND the deliverable is long, instruct Claude to ask before drafting. Bound the clarification to one question and make it conditional to prevent over-interrogation.
explanation.examTip: On clarification vs. assumption tradeoff questions, the key variable is deliverable length. Short deliverables â€” default with noted assumption. Long deliverables with foundational unknowns â€” ask first. The instruction should be conditional (`if unclear`) and bounded (`one clarifying question`).

stem: A regulatory body policy officer needs Claude to review a draft piece of secondary legislation for compliance with regulatory best-practice principles â€” including proper impact assessment, proportionality, and burden minimization. Her prompt currently just says `Review this secondary legislation and provide feedback.` Which role prompt would MOST directly activate the correct evaluative framework?

options.text: `You are a lawyer specializing in statutory compliance. Review this legislation for legal issues.`
`You are a regulatory policy expert familiar with better regulation principles, impact assessment frameworks, and the requirements of modern regulatory reform standards.`
Upload the full text of the parent statute as reference material.
Change the prompt to `Review thoroughly and flag all issues with this legislation.`

explanation.correct: Option B names the exact domain (regulatory policy) and the specific frameworks relevant to a better-regulation review (impact assessment, proportionality, burden minimization). This activates the analytical lens that evaluates whether the legislation was subject to proper impact assessment, whether it is proportionate to the policy problem, and whether it minimizes unnecessary regulatory burden â€” the dimensions of a regulatory quality review. Naming the frameworks is the activation mechanism.

distractors.A: Statutory compliance is a legal review lens â€” it checks whether the secondary legislation is within the powers of the parent Act, uses correct definitions, and follows drafting conventions. This is a different task from a better-regulation quality review. Legal compliance and regulatory policy quality are distinct frameworks.
distractors.C: Uploading the parent statute provides the vires context but is reference material, not an evaluative framework. The evaluative framework for better-regulation review comes from the role prompt specifying impact assessment and proportionality.
distractors.D: `Review thoroughly and flag all issues` is vague â€” without a specific evaluative lens, Claude reviews for general quality and may miss proportionality analysis and impact assessment gaps entirely.

explanation.concept: **Naming frameworks in role prompts as evaluative lens activation.** A role prompt that names the specific professional frameworks within a domain activates those frameworks as the evaluative lens. `Regulatory policy expert familiar with better regulation principles and impact assessment frameworks` is more precise than `regulatory expert` because it specifies which sub-domain and which analytical tools apply. The mechanism: Claude associates framework names with the criteria, vocabulary, and analytical approach associated with those frameworks in its training data. The more specific the framework reference (impact assessment, proportionality, burden minimization), the more precisely the evaluative lens matches the task.
explanation.examTip: When a role prompt needs to activate a specific evaluative framework (not just domain expertise), the role prompt must name the frameworks â€” not just the professional title. `Regulatory policy expert familiar with impact assessment frameworks` outperforms `regulatory expert` for this task.

stem: A clinical research associate at a large pharma company needs Claude to draft a site initiation visit (SIV) checklist. Her current prompt is `Write an SIV checklist.` She receives a generic clinical visit checklist. A senior colleague reviews the prompt and identifies the THREE most significant missing elements. Choose THREE

options.text: Role â€” no GCP-trained CRA persona with ICH E6(R2) expertise was specified.
Context â€” the protocol number, sponsor requirements, and site-specific regulatory obligations were not provided.
Constraints â€” no word count or length limit was specified.
Format â€” the required section structure (Regulatory Documents, Investigator Qualifications, Facilities and Equipment, Training Confirmation) was not specified.
Audience â€” no description of who will use the checklist was provided.

explanation.correct: The three primary gaps are role (GCP-trained CRA with ICH E6(R2) knowledge activates the correct regulatory vocabulary and check categories), context (the specific protocol, sponsor requirements, and site-specific obligations are proprietary â€” Claude cannot know them), and format (the required section structure must be specified to produce a usable checklist rather than a generic list). Together these three elements produce a checklist that is domain-appropriate, protocol-specific, and structurally organized for SIV use.

distractors.C: Word count is a secondary concern for a checklist â€” checklists are naturally brief by structure. Adding a word-count constraint does not address the primary content, domain knowledge, or structural gaps.
distractors.E: Audience description is secondary for a checklist â€” the checklist is a tool used by CRAs, and the role prompt (Option A) already addresses the CRA perspective. Audience description matters more for communications and educational materials where register and vocabulary must match the reader.

explanation.concept: **Three-way prompt anatomy for specialized professional tools.** Checklists for regulated clinical environments require all three primary building blocks simultaneously: role (to activate GCP and ICH E6(R2) regulatory vocabulary), context (to supply the protocol-specific and site-specific requirements that are proprietary), and format (to produce the section structure that reflects actual SIV workflow). Constraints and audience are tertiary for a checklist format. The principle: for highly regulated, protocol-specific deliverables, role + context + format are the three essential building blocks, in that order of importance. Missing any one produces output that fails on that dimension.
explanation.examTip: On three-element prompt anatomy multi-select questions, identify the primary building blocks by their impact on output correctness: role (domain vocabulary), context (proprietary specifics), format (required structure). Constraints and audience are secondary for professional tool formats like checklists.

stem: An investment management research analyst asks Claude to `Write a market analysis.` She receives a broad global overview covering multiple asset classes and geographies. She needs a focused analysis relevant to her current coverage. Which prompt would MOST effectively narrow the output to a useful research product?

options.text: Add a role prompt: `You are a senior investment research analyst with a focus on equities.`
Upload recent market data as reference material before re-prompting.
Rewrite the prompt to specify: `Write a market analysis of US mid-cap industrials equities for Q3 2024, covering P/E multiples, revenue growth rates, and free cash flow yield.`
Change the instruction to `Write a concise market analysis.`

explanation.correct: Option C provides five dimensions of specificity: geography (US), market cap segment (mid-cap), sector (industrials), time period (Q3 2024), and three specific metrics (P/E, revenue growth, FCF yield). Each specification eliminates a dimension of guesswork. The result is a research product that covers a specific analytical scope, which is both more useful and more verifiable than a global overview.

distractors.A: An equities analyst role narrows domain vocabulary but not scope â€” an equities analyst can write about any market, any geography, any sector. The role activates the right analytical approach; it does not scope the analysis to US mid-cap industrials Q3 2024.
distractors.B: Reference data improves factual accuracy but does not scope the analysis â€” if the data covers multiple markets, Claude still produces a broad analysis with more accurate data. Data and analytical scope are independent.
distractors.D: `Concise` is a length qualifier, not a scope specification. A concise global market overview is still a global market overview â€” it covers the same broad scope in fewer words.

explanation.concept: **Multi-dimensional specificity for scoped analytical tasks.** Market analyses and similar open-scope research tasks require explicit scope definition across multiple dimensions: (1) geography, (2) asset class and market cap segment, (3) sector, (4) time period, and (5) specific metrics or analytical dimensions. Each unspecified dimension generates scope creep â€” Claude includes more coverage to be thorough. Specifying all five dimensions produces a tightly scoped research product that matches coverage needs. This is especially important in investment research where the analyst has specific coverage responsibilities â€” the prompt must mirror those specific scope parameters.
explanation.examTip: When Claude produces a broad global overview for a specific analytical task, the prompt is missing multi-dimensional scope specification. Role prompts and data reference don't scope an analysis; explicit geographic, sector, time period, and metric specifications do.

stem: A luxury retail brand manager at a global fashion house needs product copy for a new leather goods collection. The Claude output is professionally written but sounds like generic premium retail copy â€” missing the brand's specific aspirational, understated, craftsmanship-forward tone. Which prompt addition would MOST directly align the output with the brand's voice?

options.text: Add a role prompt: `You are a luxury goods copywriter with 10 years of experience writing for premium fashion brands.`
Upload examples of competitor luxury brand copywriting as reference material.
Add the instruction `Write formal, sophisticated copy appropriate for a luxury brand.`

Add an explicit tone specification: `Write in our brand voice: aspirational but understated, emphasizing multi-generational craftsmanship and the emotional relationship between owner and object. Avoid promotional hyperbole and price references.`

explanation.correct: Brand-specific voice requires an explicit description of the voice's qualities â€” aspirational but understated, multi-generational craftsmanship emphasis, owner-object emotional relationship â€” plus explicit prohibitions (no hyperbole, no price references). Generic luxury copywriter role or formal/sophisticated instructions activate general luxury register, which produces professionally polished but brand-generic output. Only an explicit voice description with specific characteristics and prohibitions produces the brand-distinctive copy the manager needs.

distractors.A: A luxury goods copywriter role activates general luxury retail conventions â€” aspirational language, quality emphasis, exclusivity signals. But each luxury brand has a distinct voice within the luxury register. `Aspirational but understated with multi-generational craftsmanship focus` is a brand-specific positioning that requires explicit description, not role inference.
distractors.B: Competitor brand copywriting demonstrates other luxury brands' voices â€” which by definition are not this brand's voice. Competitor examples may actually introduce voice contamination, leading Claude toward an established competitor's register rather than this brand's distinctive positioning.
distractors.C: `Formal, sophisticated` describes the general luxury register â€” not this brand's specific voice attributes. Understated aspiration and craftsmanship-emotional focus are more specific than formality. `Formal and sophisticated` could describe many luxury brands with different voices.

explanation.concept: **Explicit brand voice description as the mechanism for distinctive copy.** A luxury copywriter role prompt activates general luxury conventions. A specific brand voice requires an explicit description of: (1) the voice's tonal qualities (aspirational but understated), (2) the thematic emphasis (multi-generational craftsmanship, owner-object relationship), and (3) explicit prohibitions (no hyperbole, no price references). The prohibition list is as important as the positive description â€” it prevents Claude from defaulting to generic luxury copy conventions that the brand specifically rejects. Brand voice specifications should be written as a brief paragraph combining positive voice attributes with specific things to avoid.
explanation.examTip: When copy sounds professionally generic for a luxury brand but not brand-specific, the role prompt is insufficient. Each luxury brand has a distinctive voice within the luxury register that requires an explicit voice specification â€” positive attributes plus specific prohibitions.

stem: A hospital system clinical documentation specialist is building a Claude workflow for generating discharge summaries from clinical notes. The current output is unstructured â€” follow-up appointments and medication reconciliation details are buried inside paragraphs rather than in clearly separated, dedicated sections. Which prompt addition would MOST directly ensure these critical elements always appear in the required locations?

options.text: Specify the required section structure with mandatory fields: `Use these sections in this order: Admission Diagnosis, Hospital Course, Discharge Diagnosis, Medications at Discharge (table format), Follow-Up Appointments, and Patient Instructions.`
Add a role prompt: `You are a clinical documentation specialist with expertise in hospital discharge processes.`
Include a sample clinical note as reference material to demonstrate the expected input format.
Add the instruction `Organize the discharge summary clearly and ensure all important information is included.`

explanation.correct: Discharge summaries must surface specific high-risk elements â€” medications and follow-up appointments â€” in dedicated, predictable locations that clinicians can quickly scan. A mandatory section structure with named fields (especially `Medications at Discharge (table format)` and `Follow-Up Appointments`) ensures these elements cannot be buried in narrative prose. The ordering instruction (`in this order`) ensures the structure is consistent across all generated summaries. This is a format specification that serves patient safety by making critical information consistently locatable.

distractors.B: A clinical documentation expert role activates general knowledge of discharge summary content but does not enforce the specific section structure that prevents medications and follow-up appointments from being buried in prose. Domain knowledge and structural enforcement are separate prompt elements.
distractors.C: A sample clinical note demonstrates the input format for Claude, not the required output structure for the discharge summary. Input format reference and output format specification are different prompt elements.
distractors.D: `Organize clearly and include all important information` is a vague quality directive. It invites Claude's own organizational judgment, which may continue to embed medication and follow-up details in narrative prose. Vague structure instructions don't enforce mandatory field locations.

explanation.concept: **Mandatory section structures for patient safety in clinical documentation.** In clinical documentation, the location of critical information matters as much as its presence. Medications at discharge and follow-up appointments buried in prose create risk â€” a clinician scanning a busy discharge summary may miss them. A mandatory section structure with named, ordered fields and format specifications (table for medications) enforces consistent information architecture across all generated documents. This is a patient-safety application of the format building block: the format is not about aesthetics but about ensuring critical information is always in a predictable, scannable location. Mandatory fields prevent summarization from collapsing or embedding required elements.
explanation.examTip: When clinical or regulatory documents bury required elements in prose, the fix is a mandatory section structure with named fields â€” not a role prompt or vague organization instruction. Mandatory fields ensure consistent information architecture.

stem: A 12-person renewable energy startup's CTO needs to draft a response to a 140-page Request for Proposals for a grid-scale battery storage project. He is planning to paste the entire RFP into the Claude prompt. Which approach is MOST appropriate for this task?

options.text: Paste the entire 140-page RFP into the prompt to ensure Claude has complete context for the response.
Extract and include only the evaluation criteria section, the technical requirements section, and the submission format requirements â€” the three sections needed to draft a compliant response.
Write a paragraph summarizing the RFP's key themes and include that summary in the prompt.
Paste the full RFP and ask Claude to identify which parts it needs to draft the response.

explanation.correct: RFP response quality depends on accurate alignment with the evaluation criteria, technical requirements, and submission format â€” not on having read every background section of the RFP. Extracting the three directly relevant sections provides Claude with everything it needs: what the evaluators will score (criteria), what must be technically addressed (requirements), and how the response must be structured (submission format). This targeted extraction improves both accuracy and focus compared to including the full 140-page document.

distractors.A: Pasting 140 pages creates context noise â€” background sections, boilerplate, and non-actionable context compete with the three sections Claude actually needs. More text does not mean better response quality when most of it is irrelevant to the drafting task.
distractors.C: A paragraph summary is too vague for technical compliance â€” it cannot capture the specific evaluation criteria weighting, the technical specification details, or the mandatory submission format requirements that determine whether the response passes evaluation.
distractors.D: Asking Claude to identify which parts it needs shifts editorial judgment to Claude and adds a round-trip before drafting. The CTO, as the subject matter expert, is better positioned to identify the relevant sections â€” this is the value of human expertise in designing the workflow.

explanation.concept: **Targeted extraction for large document workflows.** When working with large documents (RFPs, contracts, reports), the discipline is to identify which sections are directly relevant to the task and extract only those. For RFP responses: evaluation criteria (what gets scored), technical requirements (what must be addressed), submission format (how the response is structured). For contract review: change-of-control provisions, IP assignment clauses, termination rights. For regulatory submissions: the specific section of the guidance document that applies. Extracting the right three sections from a 140-page document produces better results than including the whole document because focus improves analytical precision.
explanation.examTip: For large document tasks, the question is always: which specific sections does Claude actually need to do the task? Include those, not the whole document. Targeted extraction outperforms full ingestion for analytical precision.

stem: A university press academic editor asks Claude to `Edit this 500-word book blurb and keep it under 300 words.` Claude produces a 295-word blurb that correctly satisfies the length constraint. However, the senior editor reviews it and notes it still uses academic language that will not attract a general trade audience. The academic editor asks a colleague: what element of the prompt was incomplete? What is the MOST accurate answer?

options.text: The constraint is incorrect â€” the target should have been 250 words, not 300 words.
A literary editor role would automatically produce the correct register for a trade audience.
The task specification was incomplete â€” it named the length constraint but not the register shift needed to move from academic to general trade reader vocabulary.
A format instruction specifying section headings would have organized the blurb for a trade audience.

explanation.correct: The constraint (under 300 words) was correctly specified and correctly executed â€” the output is 295 words. The gap is in the task specification: the editor wanted not just a shorter blurb but a register shift from academic vocabulary to general trade language. These are two separate dimensions â€” length and register â€” and only one was specified. The task instruction needed to include: `rewrite for a general trade reader; replace academic terminology with accessible language and emphasize the book's relevance to a non-specialist audience.`

distractors.A: The length constraint of 300 words was not the problem â€” it was correctly executed. Changing to 250 words addresses length, not the register issue that was the actual gap.
distractors.B: A literary editor role may improve general prose quality and readability, but it doesn't specifically direct Claude to shift from academic register to trade register for this specific book's audience. The register shift is a specific task requirement that must be stated.
distractors.D: Section headings are a structural format choice that can organize content but do not change vocabulary level or register. A blurb typically does not use section headings â€” and headings would not prevent academic terminology from persisting in the organized content.

explanation.concept: **Separating constraints from task specification.** Constraints (length, format, prohibited content) and task specification (what the output should accomplish) are independent building blocks. A completed constraint (295 words, under 300) does not guarantee task completion if the task itself was incompletely specified. The academic-to-trade register shift is a task specification requirement, not a constraint. The discipline: after writing a prompt, ask â€” did I specify both what the output must do (task) and what limits it must observe (constraint)? In this case, the task needed two elements: shorten AND shift register. Only one was specified.
explanation.examTip: When a length constraint is satisfied but the output still has quality problems, the task specification was incomplete â€” not the constraint. Task and constraint are separate prompt elements. Fixing the constraint number when the constraint was correctly executed is a classic trap.

stem: A non-profit education organization's curriculum developer is designing a professional development module on AI literacy for a mixed group: classroom teachers with no technical background and instructional technology coaches with moderate technical knowledge. She uses one prompt for all participants. The outputs do not differentiate content depth or expected outcomes by role. Which TWO additions would MOST effectively produce audience-appropriate differentiation? Choose TWO

options.text: Add a role prompt: `You are an AI literacy curriculum designer with experience in K-12 professional development.`
Include published research on AI in education as reference material.

Add separate audience-specific content level instructions: `For classroom teachers: focus on practical AI tool use with no technical terminology. For instructional technology coaches: include technical concepts and implementation guidance at a district level.`
Add word-count constraints allocating different lengths to each audience segment.
Add separate success criteria for each audience: `Teachers should leave able to use two AI tools in lesson planning. Coaches should leave able to evaluate and implement AI tools across a district.`

explanation.correct: Effective differentiation for a mixed audience requires both content level differentiation (what each group learns and at what depth â€” Option C) and outcome differentiation (what each group should be able to do afterward â€” Option E). Without both, the curriculum may vary in vocabulary level but miss the distinct practical competencies each role needs. Content level drives vocabulary and technical depth; success criteria drive the practical application emphasis for each audience.

distractors.A: A curriculum designer role applies equally to both audiences â€” it improves overall quality without differentiating content or outcomes by role.
distractors.B: Research reference material applies equally to both audience segments â€” it does not generate differentiated content or outcome specifications for each group.
distractors.D: Word-count allocation specifies how much content each group receives but not at what depth or with what outcome focus. Longer content for coaches without specifying technical depth or district-level outcomes produces more of the same generic content.

explanation.concept: **Two-layer differentiation for mixed audiences: content level and success criteria.** When a single module serves audiences with different backgrounds and roles, effective differentiation requires two layers: (1) content level instructions that specify vocabulary and technical depth for each audience (practical tools with no jargon vs. technical implementation guidance), and (2) success criteria that specify what each audience should be able to do after the module (individual lesson planning vs. district-level implementation). Without both layers, differentiation is incomplete â€” vocabulary may vary while outcomes remain undifferentiated, or outcomes may differ while content is still pitched at the same technical level.
explanation.examTip: On multi-audience differentiation questions, look for both the content depth instruction and the success criteria instruction. One without the other produces incomplete differentiation. Both are needed together for effective role-based audience separation.

stem: An actuarial manager at a large life insurer is using Claude to draft sections of a mortality assumption validation report. The output lacks technical depth and does not reference the professional standards that govern actuarial validation work. Which role prompt would MOST directly produce the required actuarial standard of practice framing?

options.text: `You are an insurance analytics expert with experience in mortality and morbidity modeling.`
Upload the most recent industry mortality tables as reference material.
Add the instruction `Be more technical and rigorous in your analysis of mortality assumptions.`

`You are an FSA-credentialed actuary specializing in mortality experience studies. Frame your analysis using ASOP No. 25 standards for credibility and comply with actuarial standard of practice documentation requirements.`

explanation.correct: Option D names two specifics that activate the correct professional framework: FSA credentialing (the professional credential governing life insurance actuarial practice) and ASOP No. 25 (the specific actuarial standard of practice covering credibility procedures for mortality experience studies). Naming the specific ASOP activates the analytical dimensions that standard requires â€” credibility weighting, experience period, graduated vs. crude rates â€” which are the dimensions missing from the generic output. The professional standard name is the activation signal.

distractors.A: `Insurance analytics expert` is a broad domain role that activates general data analysis and modeling vocabulary but does not activate the specific actuarial professional standards framework (ASOP standards, credibility procedures, professional documentation requirements) that the validation report requires.
distractors.B: Industry mortality tables provide benchmarking data but do not supply the analytical framework or professional standard framing. Data and framework are separate inputs.
distractors.C: `Be more technical and rigorous` is a vague quality directive without specifying the standard or framework. Claude applies more detailed analysis but doesn't know which professional standard to apply â€” the output may be technically detailed without being ASOP-compliant.

explanation.concept: **Naming professional standards in role prompts for regulated outputs.** When output must comply with a specific professional standard â€” an actuarial standard of practice, a clinical practice guideline, a regulatory framework â€” the role prompt should name the standard explicitly. The standard name activates the analytical criteria, documentation requirements, and professional vocabulary associated with that standard. The pattern: `You are a [credentialed professional] specializing in [domain]. Apply [specific standard/framework] and comply with [documentation requirements].` This produces output that reflects the professional standard's requirements rather than general domain best practices.
explanation.examTip: When technical output lacks professional standard framing, the role prompt needs to name the specific standard (ASOP No. 25, ICH E6(R2), ISO 9001 Section 10.2) â€” not just the job title or domain. Standard names are the activation signals for regulated analytical frameworks.

stem: An aerospace manufacturing systems integration engineer at a Tier-1 supplier asks Claude to help draft a change request document for the company's `MES-7 integration layer` connecting to the `APQP Phase 3 gateway`. Claude produces a generic change request template that mentions neither MES-7 nor APQP Phase 3. The engineer needs to fix the prompt. What is the PRIMARY cause of the generic output?

options.text: The MES-7 integration layer specifications and the company's APQP Phase 3 gateway requirements are proprietary definitions that were not provided; Claude filled in generic change request content because it has no knowledge of these systems.
The aerospace systems engineer role was not specified; adding it would activate knowledge of MES and APQP systems.
The AS9100 quality management standard was not uploaded as reference material; it defines change request requirements for aerospace suppliers.
The instruction `Be more specific and technical` in a follow-up message would supply the missing system context.

explanation.correct: `MES-7` and `APQP Phase 3 gateway` are proprietary internal system and process names that exist only within this company. They are not referenced in any publicly available aerospace or manufacturing literature that would be in Claude's training data. Without definitions â€” what MES-7 is, what the integration layer does, what APQP Phase 3 gate requirements the company uses â€” Claude produces a generic change request because it has no basis for anything more specific. The fix is to define both systems in the prompt.

distractors.B: An aerospace systems engineer role activates general aerospace vocabulary (APQP as a general concept, MES as a category) but cannot supply the proprietary specifications of this company's MES-7 system or their specific APQP Phase 3 gate requirements. General domain knowledge and proprietary system specifications are different.
distractors.C: AS9100 defines general change management requirements for aerospace quality systems but not this company's specific MES-7 or APQP gateway implementation. Public standards and proprietary system specs are different.
distractors.D: `Be more specific and technical` asks Claude to do more with the same absent data â€” without the system definitions, Claude produces more detailed generic change request language, not MES-7-specific content.

explanation.concept: **Proprietary system names as invisible context gaps.** Engineers who work daily with proprietary systems forget that system names (MES-7, APQP Phase 3 gateway, CRM-7 integration layer) are opaque to anyone outside the organization. These names appear in their prompts without definitions because the context is obvious to the engineer â€” but Claude has never encountered these system names in any form. The fix is a brief system description: `MES-7 is our manufacturing execution system that [specific function]. The APQP Phase 3 gateway is our internal milestone review process requiring [specific outputs].` This context transforms a generic change request template into a system-specific document.
explanation.examTip: When outputs are generic despite specific system or process names in the prompt, the cause is always missing proprietary definitions â€” not role or reference standard. Internal system names are invisible context gaps that must be defined explicitly.

stem: A bid manager at a 45,000-employee telecoms company is using Claude to help write proposals. Her current prompt is `Write the executive summary for this proposal.` She receives a generic executive summary. A senior colleague reviews the prompt and identifies the TWO improvements that would have the MOST impact on output quality. Choose TWO

options.text: Role â€” `You are a senior bid manager experienced with telecoms infrastructure proposals for government clients.`
Word-count constraint of 400 words maximum.
Reference to the full RFP document.
Format â€” `Structure the executive summary with these sections: Client Situation, Proposed Solution, Key Differentiators, Pricing Summary, and Implementation Timeline.`
Audience description of the procurement committee evaluation panel.

explanation.correct: The two highest-impact improvements are role (activating bid management expertise specific to telecoms infrastructure and government procurement contexts) and format (specifying the five required executive summary sections that structure the document appropriately for a proposal review process).
